en: The disciple said:
Since the non-dual state remains whole, as existence-consciousness-bliss, free from conceptual construction and of a single nature, how can worship be performed?

Where is there an invocation for the Full One? Where is there a seat for the Support of All? Where is there water for the feet for the Transparent One? And from where can there be water for sipping for the Pure One? (2)
How can there be bathing for one who is stainless? How can there be clothing for one whose belly is the universe? And how can there be a sacred thread for one who has neither lineage nor caste? (3)

How can there be fragrance for that which is unstained? And what flower for that which is scentless? What ornament for that which is without distinction? What decoration for that which is formless? (4)
What need is there for incense or lamps for the stainless one, the witness of all?
What could be an offering of food here for him who is satisfied solely by his own bliss? (5)
What betel leaf could be prepared for Him, the delighter of the universe, who is the self-luminous form of consciousness and the illuminator of the sun and other luminaries? (6)
How could there be a ritual of waving lights (nīrājana) for Him who is praised by the Vedas?
Circumambulation belongs to the Infinite; prostration belongs to the Non-dual Reality. (7)
What praise can be prescribed for Him who is unknowable even by the words of the Vedas?
And whence could there be a rite for dismissal for Him who abides both within and without? (8)
The Guru said:
I worship my own liṅga, which resembles a jewel,
seated within the lotus at the heart of the city of Māyā,
through the consecrations of the pure water of the mind from the river of faith.
Constantly with the flowers of meditative concentration, for the sake of no further rebirth. || 9 ||
Thinking, "I alone remain," one should thus invoke Śiva;
thereafter, one should prepare a seat and contemplate one's own self as being firmly established.
"O wise one, one should offer water for the feet, which destroys all impurities, with the realization: 'I have no attachment to the dust of merit or sin.'"
One should offer a handful of water to the emblem of the Self, casting away the root-ignorance sustained since beginningless kalpas; that indeed is the presentation of the arghya offering.

The meditative visualization (dhyāna) and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) are considered to be drinking even a minute fraction— a mere ten-millionth part of a wave from the ocean of the bliss of Brahman— by Indra and the other gods.
All the worlds are completely drenched by the very water of the bliss of Brahman;
the meditation that "this Self is indestructible" is the consecration of the self. 14.
The sage should contemplate thus: "I am the light of unobscured consciousness"; this is the true garment of the mark of the Self. || 15 ||
"I am the thread that strings together the entire garland of worlds, whose nature consists of the three qualities"—
this very certainty is indeed considered here to be the supreme sacred thread (upavīta).

"This manifold world, mixed with manifold latent impressions, has been sustained by me alone and not by another"—this reflection upon the Self would be like sandalwood [cooling the fever of worldly existence]. (17)

One should daily worship the symbol of the Self with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains— which take the form of the abandonment of the fluctuations of rajas, sattva, and tamas— in order to achieve liberation while living.
One should worship Śiva as the self-liṅga with non-dual bilva leaves, free from the threefold distinctions of "the Lord," "the guru," and "the self. (19)
The wise one should contemplate the incense as the abandonment of all latent impressions (vāsanās),
and should display the lamp as the self-knowledge consisting of light.
The great rice-offering for one's own *liṅga* is that which is called the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*);
drink its sweet essence of bliss, with death as its condiment. (21)

One should remember that for the hand of the Self-symptom (ātma-liṅga), which has been soiled by ignorance, the washing with the water of knowledge is the cleansing of the hands once it has become pure. 22.
For Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is devoid of qualities such as passion,
the abandonment of the practice of passionate objects is like the chewing of betel.
The knowledge of one's own nature as Brahman is the sun of fierce intelligence that destroys the darkness of ignorance; it is the ritual lustration of the self in this world. (24)
One should contemplate the handful of flowers as being adorned with garlands that manifest the vision of the manifold Brahman, and as embodying the vision of the nature of perfect bliss. 25.
"Thousands of cosmic eggs revolve within me, the Lord;
'I am the immutable, immovable form'—this meditation is the circumambulation. (26)
"I alone am the one to be worshipped by the universe; there is no one other than me to be worshipped"—this very realization is here the worship of the Linga of one's own Self. (27)

The honoring of the self is said to consist in the contemplation of the non-existence of things to be done; the chanting of the Name consists in the meditation on the Self that has transcended name and form. (28)

Listening to that God is the contemplation on the non-existence of anything to be heard; reflection, however, is the contemplation on the non-existence of anything to be reflected upon regarding the mark of the Self. (29)
The consciousness of the non-existence of that which is to be meditated upon is the profound contemplation (nididhyāsana) of the Self;
it is the state of being established in the Self through the total absence of delusion and mental distraction. (30)
Samādhi is the very name of the Self; it is nothing other than the cessation of the mind's delusion.
In that very Brahman, the perpetual resting of the mind is what is intended.
Thus, worshipping the linga of one's own self as described in the Vedāntakalpa, whether until death or even for a single moment, being well-composed; || 32 ||
One should cast off the entire web of evil latent impressions like dust from one's feet;
having shaken off the flood of suffering born of ignorance, one attains the bliss of liberation.

Thus ends the Nirguṇamānasapūjā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the wandering mendicants of the supreme order (Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).
